strengths: The double-logarithmic priority bucketing is simple and mathematically motivated. Section 3 provides a clear, reusable argument connecting polynomial growth in score counts to logarithmic expected depth, subject to the boundary corrections noted below.

The static-frequency construction accommodates arbitrary key orders and frequency distributions, removing the restrictions attributed to LLW22. The counterexamples in Section 4.2 give useful insight into why deterministic frequency priorities and single-logarithmic bucketing can perform poorly.

Future working-set size is a well-motivated prediction target. Its relationship to current recency ranks provides a useful smoothness argument, and Theorem 4.6 supplies a meaningful cross-entropy bound for frequency predictions.
weaknesses: The dynamic runtime proofs rely on Lemma 2.3, which is false as stated: deleting a treap node need not cost O(depth(x)). A constant-depth root can require merging long boundary paths of its subtrees. In particular, deleting a uniquely high-priority median above otherwise uniformly randomized priorities requires Θ(log n) expected merge work. Consequently, the delete-and-reinsert implementation does not establish the maintenance bounds used in Theorems 5.5 and 5.7. Direct priority changes through rotations may repair this issue, but the operation and its analysis must be supplied.

Corollary 4.7's O(m·DKL(p,q)) excess-cost claim is false as a comparison with the tree built using p. For three ordered keys, let p=(3/8,1/4+ε,3/8−ε) and q=(3/8,1/4−ε,3/8+ε), for sufficiently small ε>0. The expected depth under p increases by 4ε/3 per access when using q, whereas DKL(p,q)=Θ(ε²). The cross-entropy theorem provides an upper bound involving H(p)+DKL(p,q); subtracting asymptotic upper bounds does not establish the claimed excess cost.

Originality is insufficiently established against classical weighted randomized search trees. Weighted treaps already provide expected depth O(1+log(W/w_x)); choosing weights equal to predicted frequencies yields static-optimality and cross-entropy bounds for arbitrary key orders. The paper should explain what the proposed bucketing and working-set reductions add beyond this machinery. Showing that two simpler priority assignments fail does not resolve this comparison.

The past-working-set result remains conditional on an uncontrolled maintenance cost. Theorem 5.7 includes the additional sum over changed scores, but no maintenance procedure bounds this term by the working-set access budget. The theorem acknowledges this limitation; the broader claims about achieving the working-set bound should preserve it.

The robustness claims exceed the guarantees demonstrated. The future-advice theorem assumes polynomial accuracy at every access, and the static cross-entropy bound provides no prediction-independent O(log n) fallback. Sufficiently inaccurate frequency predictions can still produce linear-depth trees. The paper should distinguish tolerance within its stated accuracy assumptions from robustness to arbitrary erroneous advice.

There are repairable but pervasive boundary errors. Consecutive accesses permit work(i)=0, making the priority expression log log(s(i)+1) undefined under the required prediction guarantee. The stated total bound also omits the unavoidable Ω(m) processing cost for repeated accesses. Scores need explicit clipping, and access bounds need additive constants; similarly, the entropy runtime requires an additive m term. These corrections should be propagated through the theorem statements and proofs.
